quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Physical education should be compulsory for all students throughout secondary school.
options: Compulsory PE ensures every student receives regular physical activity regardless of background.
Structured PE teaches teamwork, fair play, and resilience that benefit students across all subjects.
Older teenagers should have the freedom to choose activities they genuinely enjoy and value.
Forcing uninterested students through PE can create a lasting aversion to all forms of exercise.
quests.hint: Think about why compulsory PE benefits all students (Pros) and what it costs reluctant participants (Cons).
quests.explanation: Mandatory PE guarantees activity and teaches social skills for every student (Pros), but removing student choice can generate lasting resentment and aversion to exercise in those who find competitive sports distressing (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Regular physical education improves students' academic performance across all subjects.
options: Physical activity increases blood flow to the brain, directly enhancing cognitive function and memory.
Students who exercise regularly demonstrate better concentration and behaviour in academic lessons.
Time allocated to PE directly reduces the hours available for academic subject teaching.
The academic benefits of exercise can be achieved through active commuting without formal PE lessons.
quests.hint: Consider whether compulsory PE genuinely supports academic achievement (Pros) and whether the time cost is justified (Cons).
quests.explanation: Exercise boosts brain function and classroom concentration (Pros), but PE reduces academic teaching hours, and similar benefits could come from active travel and unstructured break time (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Making PE compulsory addresses the public health crisis of youth inactivity.
options: Compulsory school PE is one of the few guaranteed touchpoints for physical activity in young people's lives.
Building exercise habits during adolescence significantly reduces the risk of adult obesity and disease.
School PE sessions alone are insufficient to meet recommended daily physical activity guidelines.
Addressing youth inactivity requires broader community investment, not just school PE provision.
quests.hint: Think about PE's role in public health (Pros) and whether it is sufficient on its own (Cons).
quests.explanation: Compulsory PE is a reliable way to build activity habits and reduce obesity risk (Pros), but PE alone falls far short of recommended daily activity levels, and systemic inactivity requires community-wide solutions beyond school sport (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: The school day should be shortened by one hour to reduce student stress.
options: A shorter day gives students essential time to rest, pursue interests, and recover from intensive learning.
Reducing daily time pressure may improve the quality and depth of learning during the hours that remain.
A shorter school day reduces total teaching time, potentially harming academic outcomes for all students.
Students from difficult home environments particularly benefit from the extended safe school structure.
quests.hint: Think about what a shorter school day gives students (Pros) and who it might disadvantage (Cons).
quests.explanation: A shorter day provides recovery time and may improve remaining learning quality (Pros), but reduced teaching time risks academic harm and removes a vital structured environment for students from difficult home situations (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Shorter school days can significantly improve teacher wellbeing and professional retention.
options: Reducing teacher working hours improves job satisfaction and lowers unsustainable burnout rates.
Better-rested, less stressed teachers are more effective, enthusiastic, and engaging in the classroom.
Shorter days reduce the ability to cover required curriculum content within the school year.
Teacher wellbeing is better improved through better pay and workload support rather than fewer teaching hours.
quests.hint: Consider the teacher wellbeing case for shorter days (Pros) and alternative ways to support staff effectively (Cons).
quests.explanation: Fewer hours reduce burnout and improve teacher effectiveness (Pros), but shorter days sacrifice curriculum coverage, and teacher wellbeing could be addressed more effectively through pay reform and professional development (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: A shorter school day creates time for extracurricular activities and healthy family life.
options: Earlier school finishes give students time for clubs, sport, creative hobbies, and shared family meals.
Balanced daily schedules that include downtime produce more well-rounded and emotionally resilient young people.
Many working parents depend on school as supervised childcare throughout the standard working day.
High-achieving school systems internationally often feature longer, not shorter, school days.
quests.hint: Think about the lifestyle benefits of a shorter day (Pros) and the practical and international concerns (Cons).
quests.explanation: Shorter days create space for enrichment activities and family connection (Pros), but working parents depend on school for childcare, and many high-performing education systems demonstrate that longer days can produce excellent outcomes (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Secondary school students should be allowed to choose their own subjects freely.
options: Student autonomy in subject choice significantly increases motivation and genuine engagement in learning.
Allowing personal choice produces graduates with deeper expertise and passion in their chosen fields.
Young teenagers often lack the maturity and information to make sound long-term educational decisions.
Free subject choice creates social pressure where students avoid subjects considered academically unfashionable.
quests.hint: Think about the motivational benefits of student subject choice (Pros) and the risks of early autonomy (Cons).
quests.explanation: Student-chosen subjects boost motivation and build genuine expertise (Pros), but teenagers may lack the maturity to choose wisely, and social pressure can push them towards fashionable rather than individually appropriate subjects (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: A compulsory core curriculum ensures a broad and balanced education for all students.
options: Required subjects expose every student to essential knowledge across all disciplines without exception.
Structured curriculum prevents students from avoiding challenging subjects they might need in the future.
Rigid compulsory curricula deny students the agency that research consistently shows improves performance.
Breadth requirements can result in surface-level coverage rather than genuine depth of understanding.
quests.hint: Consider the arguments for compulsory breadth versus student-chosen specialisation in school curricula.
quests.explanation: Compulsory subjects guarantee breadth and prevent knowledge gaps (Pros for structure), but rigid curricula undermine motivation and can produce wide but shallow learning rather than genuine understanding (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Allowing students to choose subjects better prepares them for adult and career life.
options: Students who choose relevant subjects arrive at university or employment significantly better prepared.
Making meaningful educational choices at school develops the decision-making skills needed in adult life.
Early specialisation limits future flexibility and may permanently close off career pathways.
Students who drop foundational subjects too early may face significant knowledge gaps later in life.
quests.hint: Think about how subject choice prepares students for the future (Pros) and the risks of over-specialising early (Cons).
quests.explanation: Relevant subject choice improves preparedness and builds adult decision-making capacity (Pros), but early specialisation narrows future options and can leave students with fundamental knowledge gaps they cannot easily recover (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Schools should adopt a four-day week to benefit students and teaching staff.
options: An extra rest day each week allows students and teachers to recharge and pursue personal interests.
Evidence from pilot schools suggests academic outcomes remain stable or even improve on a four-day week.
A four-day week creates significant childcare problems for parents who work a standard five-day schedule.
Schools may struggle to deliver the full required curriculum in twenty percent less contact time.
quests.hint: Think about the wellbeing case for a four-day school week (Pros) and the practical problems it creates (Cons).
quests.explanation: Four-day weeks promote wellbeing, and pilots show stable academic results (Pros), but working parents face childcare gaps and schools risk being unable to cover the full required curriculum in fewer days (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: A four-day school week reduces teacher burnout and significantly improves staff retention.
options: Shorter weeks substantially reduce the stress and exhaustion that are driving teachers out of the profession.
Retaining experienced teachers through better conditions directly improves educational quality for students.
Reducing teaching days increases the pressure on each remaining school day, potentially raising daily stress.
Teacher retention problems are better addressed through salary increases and reduced administrative workload.
quests.hint: Consider whether a four-day week genuinely improves teacher retention (Pros) and the alternative solutions (Cons).
quests.explanation: Shorter weeks reduce burnout and help retain experienced teachers (Pros), but condensed schedules may increase daily pressure, and pay increases and administrative relief may be more targeted and effective solutions (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: A four-day school week actively supports student mental health and reduces anxiety levels.
options: A three-day weekend gives students recovering from mental health difficulties more time to stabilise.
Reduced school pressure allows students to develop personal interests and social connections outside school.
Students in difficult home situations depend on school for safety, structured routine, and meals five days a week.
Extended school breaks may increase inequality as wealthier families provide richer out-of-school experiences.
quests.hint: Think about the mental health case for a four-day week (Pros) and who it may leave behind (Cons).
quests.explanation: Extra rest days support mental health recovery and personal development (Pros), but vulnerable students depend on school structure five days a week, and longer breaks risk deepening the inequality between advantaged and disadvantaged students (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Music and art should be compulsory subjects throughout secondary school.
options: Creative subjects develop imagination, problem-solving, and aesthetic sensibility in every student.
Compulsory arts education gives all students a platform for emotional expression and self-discovery.
Mandatory creative subjects reduce time available for STEM and other academic priorities.
Students who are clearly uninterested in arts may resent being required to study them.
quests.hint: Think about the value of universal arts education (Pros) and what it costs in terms of curriculum time (Cons).
quests.explanation: Compulsory arts build creativity and emotional expression for every student (Pros), but they reduce STEM time, and forcing disengaged students through arts lessons may produce resentment rather than appreciation (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Compulsory music education builds cognitive skills that benefit all academic subjects.
options: Learning to read music and play instruments strengthens mathematical reasoning and working memory.
Music education develops disciplined practice habits that support learning across all subjects.
The cognitive benefits attributed to music can be equally well achieved through other rigorous subjects.
Students already receiving private instrument tuition gain little additional benefit from compulsory school music.
quests.hint: Consider whether compulsory music uniquely builds cognitive skills (Pros) and whether those skills are music-specific (Cons).
quests.explanation: Music strengthens mathematical reasoning and builds disciplined practice habits (Pros), but those cognitive gains are achievable through other subjects, and musically experienced students may find compulsory school music lessons unrewarding (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Art and music education preserves cultural heritage and identity for young people.
options: Studying artistic traditions connects students to their cultural history and national heritage.
Creative subjects develop cultural literacy that helps students engage thoughtfully with diverse global societies.
Cultural heritage can be effectively transmitted through history, literature, and other subjects.
Arts curricula often reflect majority cultural traditions, potentially marginalising minority students.
quests.hint: Think about arts education as cultural preservation (Pros) and whose culture it may or may not represent (Cons).
quests.explanation: Arts education connects students to cultural heritage and builds global cultural literacy (Pros), but culture can be taught through other subjects, and dominant cultural traditions in arts curricula may marginalise minority students' identities (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Schools should replace all printed textbooks with digital tablets for learning.
options: Tablets provide instant access to up-to-date information, eliminating the problem of outdated textbooks.
Interactive digital content can adapt to individual students' learning speeds and comprehension levels.
Tablets are costly to purchase, maintain, and replace, creating a significant ongoing financial burden.
Screen-based reading is consistently associated with lower comprehension than reading from print.
quests.hint: Think about the benefits of replacing textbooks with tablets (Pros) and the costs and learning risks (Cons).
quests.explanation: Tablets offer current information and adaptive learning (Pros), but high device costs and evidence that screen reading produces lower comprehension than print are significant drawbacks (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Digital tablets make school resources more accessible and equitable for all learners.
options: A single tablet can hold every textbook a student needs, significantly reducing the weight of school bags.
Tablets can be updated instantly to reflect curriculum changes without expensive new print runs.
Not all students have reliable home internet access, creating a digital divide in out-of-school use.
Students from disadvantaged backgrounds may be less able to replace expensive damaged or stolen devices.
quests.hint: Consider how tablets improve access (Pros) and how they risk widening educational inequality (Cons).
quests.explanation: Tablets reduce physical burden and lower long-term resource update costs (Pros), but internet inequality at home and the financial impact of device loss create new forms of educational disadvantage (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Printed textbooks provide a more reliable and focused learning environment than screens.
options: Physical books do not require charging, internet connectivity, or technical support to function.
Reading print is less distracting than devices, which students can use to access games and social media.
Printed textbooks become outdated quickly and are expensive to replace across a whole school system.
Students who learn to navigate physical reference materials develop valuable research skills.
quests.hint: Think about the reliability advantages of printed textbooks (Pros for keeping them) and their long-term costs (Cons).
quests.explanation: Print requires no power or connectivity and creates a more focused reading environment (Pros for keeping books), but textbooks become outdated rapidly and are costly to update at scale (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Well-behaved dogs should be permitted in office workplaces.
options: Studies consistently show that the presence of dogs in offices significantly reduces employee stress levels.
Office dogs create natural opportunities for conversation and improve social bonds between colleagues.
Dog allergies and phobias affect a significant proportion of the working population.
Dogs can be disruptive, unpredictable, or noisy, undermining professional concentration and focus.
quests.hint: Think about the wellbeing benefits of office dogs (Pros) and the problems they create for other employees (Cons).
quests.explanation: Office dogs reduce stress and improve colleague interaction and morale (Pros), but allergies, phobias, and disruptive animal behaviour make them incompatible with many professional environments (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Allowing dogs in offices improves employee retention and overall job satisfaction.
options: Unique workplace perks like pet-friendly policies attract talent and signal a modern, progressive culture.
Employees who can bring their dogs to work save on dog care costs and experience less separation anxiety.
Dog-friendly policies require significant investment in clear guidelines and appropriate facilities.
Non-dog-owning employees may feel a pet-friendly policy disproportionately benefits dog owners only.
quests.hint: Consider whether dog-friendly offices genuinely improve workplace culture (Pros) and the equity concerns (Cons).
quests.explanation: Pet-friendly workplaces attract talent and reduce dog owner stress and costs (Pros), but implementation requires infrastructure, and non-pet-owning employees may perceive the policy as unfair and exclusionary (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Dog-friendly offices are inappropriate in most professional working environments.
options: Many professional settings require the level of quiet and focus that is incompatible with dog behaviour.
Health and safety regulations in many workplaces make the permanent presence of animals legally problematic.
With clear workplace guidelines and designated areas, dogs can be managed without disrupting operations.
Some employers successfully allow dogs only on specific days, creating a workable and inclusive compromise.
quests.hint: Think about why dogs may not suit most offices (Pros for restriction) and the available compromises (Cons).
quests.explanation: Professional environments require focus and may face legal obstacles to permanent animal presence (Pros for restriction), but clear rules, designated areas, or dog-friendly days offer workable middle-ground solutions (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Employers should offer flexible starting and finishing times to all office workers.
options: Flexible hours allow employees to work during their natural peak hours of energy and cognitive focus.
Removing rigid hour requirements reduces stressful rush-hour commuting and travel time.
Team coordination becomes significantly harder when colleagues work different daily schedules.
Customer-facing roles require standard hours that flexible working arrangements cannot easily accommodate.
quests.hint: Think about how flexible hours benefit employees (Pros) and the coordination challenges they create (Cons).
quests.explanation: Flexible hours match work to natural productivity rhythms and reduce commuting stress (Pros), but team coordination suffers when colleagues are not simultaneously available, and customer-facing roles cannot easily adopt flexible arrangements (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Flexible working hours significantly improve employee mental health and work-life balance.
options: Control over working hours reduces the chronic stress of rigid scheduling that affects personal life.
Flexibility allows employees to attend medical appointments, school events, and family commitments.
Employers cannot always guarantee that flexible workers will be available for genuinely urgent requirements.
Inequitable access to flexible arrangements between office and frontline staff can create workplace resentment.
quests.hint: Consider how flexibility supports wellbeing (Pros) and the inequities it can create between staff types (Cons).
quests.explanation: Schedule control reduces stress and allows employees to meet personal obligations (Pros), but flexibility is hard to guarantee in urgent situations, and unequal access between office and frontline staff breeds resentment (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Flexible hours increase employee productivity and meaningfully reduce absenteeism.
options: Employees who control their own schedules consistently report higher job satisfaction and engagement.
Flexibility reduces sick leave by allowing staff to proactively manage health and personal needs.
Without clear boundaries, flexible workers often end up working significantly longer than their contracted hours.
Measuring productivity fairly becomes more complex when employees are working to different daily patterns.
quests.hint: Think about how flexibility affects output and attendance (Pros) and the overwork and measurement risks (Cons).
quests.explanation: Schedule autonomy raises satisfaction and reduces absenteeism (Pros), but without boundaries flexible workers tend to overwork, and tracking performance across varied schedules is significantly more complex for employers (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: All public transport should be made completely free of charge for every user.
options: Free public transport removes the financial barrier to mobility for lower-income citizens.
Free networks dramatically increase ridership, reducing private car use and carbon emissions.
Free transport must be funded through general taxation, redistributing the cost to all citizens.
Heavily subsidised networks risk becoming overcrowded and under-resourced without sufficient revenue.
quests.hint: Think about the equity and environmental case for free transport (Pros) and the funding challenges (Cons).
quests.explanation: Free transport improves mobility for low-income citizens and boosts ridership to reduce emissions (Pros), but the tax burden on all citizens and the risk of overcrowded, under-resourced networks are serious practical concerns (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Free public transport would significantly reduce air pollution in cities and towns.
options: Removing the cost barrier would shift millions of car journeys onto buses and trains each day.
Better urban air quality from modal shift improves public health, reducing healthcare costs.
Free fares alone do not address the poor reliability and infrequency that deter many car users.
Significant service improvement investment is required before free fares can effectively replace car trips.
quests.hint: Consider whether free fares alone are sufficient to cut urban pollution (Pros) and what else is needed (Cons).
quests.explanation: Free fares shift car users to public transport, improving air quality (Pros), but poor service reliability deters mode shift, and service investment must accompany fare removal to achieve meaningful emission reductions (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Free public transport strengthens social cohesion and reduces inequality across communities.
options: Universal free access gives everyone equal freedom to participate in community and economic life.
Free networks allow lower-income individuals to access employment, healthcare, and education freely.
Wealthy people who easily afford fares would benefit from free transport unnecessarily.
The same public funding redirected from free transport could deliver greater social benefit if targeted.
quests.hint: Think about free transport as a social equity policy (Pros) and whether it is the most efficient use of funds (Cons).
quests.explanation: Free universal transport promotes equal participation and supports low-income access to opportunity (Pros), but subsidising wealthy users who do not need support is inefficient, and targeted spending might deliver greater social return (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Single-use plastic should be banned in all shops, cafes, and restaurants.
options: Eliminating single-use plastic at the point of sale directly reduces plastic waste entering ecosystems.
A ban pushes businesses and consumers to develop and adopt more sustainable packaging alternatives.
Small businesses face significant costs in sourcing and switching to sustainable packaging materials.
A partial ban on retail plastic has limited impact if it continues to be used widely in other sectors.
quests.hint: Think about the environmental case for banning single-use retail plastic (Pros) and the economic and scope concerns (Cons).
quests.explanation: Banning single-use plastic reduces ecosystem pollution and drives innovation in sustainable packaging (Pros), but small businesses face real cost pressures, and sector-only bans have limited effect while plastic persists in other industries (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: Banning single-use plastic encourages broader cultural change towards sustainable consumption.
options: A high-profile and widely discussed ban raises public awareness of the global plastic pollution crisis.
Policy bans normalise sustainable behaviour, making environmentally responsible choices the default option.
Cultural change driven by legislation can feel coercive and generate significant public resistance.
Industry lobbying frequently weakens plastic bans, creating loopholes that severely undermine environmental impact.
quests.hint: Consider whether plastic bans genuinely drive cultural change (Pros) and the risks of legislative enforcement (Cons).
quests.explanation: High-profile bans raise awareness and normalise sustainability as a default (Pros), but coercive policy can generate resistance, and industry lobbying produces diluted bans with major loopholes that reduce environmental benefit (Cons).

quests.instruction: Weigh the arguments as pros (support) or cons (counter).
quests.prompt: A ban on single-use plastic protects marine ecosystems and wildlife from serious harm.
options: Millions of tonnes of plastic enter oceans annually, killing marine animals and entering the food chain.
Reducing plastic at source is the most direct and reliable way to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems.
Most ocean plastic originates in countries without effective waste management or plastic bans.
Many supposedly biodegradable alternatives are not genuinely better for the environment across their full lifecycle.
quests.hint: Think about the marine conservation case for plastic bans (Pros) and the limits of national-level action (Cons).
quests.explanation: Reducing retail plastic at source directly protects marine life (Pros), but most ocean plastic comes from countries without effective bans, and supposedly greener alternatives are not always environmentally superior when their full production is considered (Cons).
